back: Being able to produce more of a good than another country using the same quantity of resources.
Being able to produce a good at a lower opportunity cost than another country.
The quantity and quality of land, labour, capital and enterprise that a country has.

front: How do you find the opportunity cost of good X from an output table?
back: Output of good Y given up ÷ output of good X gained (with the same resources).

front: Can a country have the comparative advantage in both of two goods?
back: No. Its two opportunity costs are reciprocals, so a lower cost in one good means a higher cost in the other.

front: Country A has the absolute advantage in both goods. Can trade still benefit both countries?
back: Yes, if opportunity costs differ: each specialises where its opportunity cost is lower and trades at a rate between the two costs.

front: Which trade rate lets both countries gain?
back: Any rate strictly between the two countries' opportunity costs of the good.

front: Give three limitations of the theory of comparative advantage.
back: Transport costs; immobile resources; rising opportunity costs; trade barriers; risk of depending on a few exports.
A country concentrating its resources on the goods it can produce at the lowest (opportunity) cost and trading for other goods.
